newsitem.title: GERMANY: German liability insurers must co-operate-Schilling.
newsitem.headline: German liability insurers must co-operate-Schilling.

text.p: Industry and liability insurers must "stick together even in tough times" and have "nerves of steel and show strong endurance" to sustain catastrophe liabilities, the Cologne risk management conference was told on Thursday.

Herbert Schilling of Gerling-Konzern, the chairman of the liability committee of the German insurance federation, also said that insurance customers should create a strong public image and learn to deal with alleged, but unfounded claims, class actions and large numbers of claimants.
"Have sufficient documentation of product development and manufacturing, but do not retain documentary paperwork demonstrating product defects," said Schilling.

"One of our clients lost a costly lawsuit when the claimant's lawyer produced a paper showing some weakness in a car during an unsuccessful test run. The leading engineer had years ago thrown this paper into the waste-basket."
He also advised that companies should have the highest affordable insurance limit. "For liability, there is no ceiling, not even for smaller companies."
Insurers should have the best internationally experienced staff. "If you feel this is too costly, you'd better leave the field of industrial liability to your competitors," he said.

Insurers should maintain close contacts with insureds, including top management, should constantly monitor technical, legal and scientific trends and develop alternative strategies in defending claims.
Industry and insurers were today faced with tighter legal liability conditions worldwide, Schilling said.

"The job of politicians is to make law. In our field, this means to create legal liability. During the last four decades, this activity has substantially aggravated the liability burden for manufacturers and plant owners in Germany."
In the public eye, the claimant is always seen as the good guy who deserves any help at the expense of the defendant, said Schilling.
This was so in cases such as those of AIDS sufferers who contracted the virus through blood products, where the claims had been handled correctly by insurers.
"This did not stop politicians from mounting a massive two-year attack against the liability insurers of the pharmaceutical companies."

Insurers also face an increasing claims potential due to the rising number of identical products, as well as contradicting expert opinions in assessing causation links and relevant health injury consequences.
Schilling blamed an increasing claims consciousness, as well as a general decline in assuming personal responsibility.
"If you buy a batman cape for your son, don't expect him to be able to fly," he said, but added that this was often not the public's attitude.
There was also insufficient knowledge of product-related diseases. Schilling added that even big corporations show financial and psychological weakness when facing huge claims.

Earlier, Willi Suter, head of the international division of Swiss insurer Winterthur, had told the conference that the traditional co-operation of insureds, brokers and insurers was no longer sufficient to cope with market demands.
Captive brokers are increasingly becoming risk managers, brokers risk consultants and insurers problem solvers, rather than product suppliers.
He advocated "interactive risk management", reducing costs and securing a faster flow of information.
-- Herbert Fromme, Reuters Insurance News, +49 221 512007
